title: A Physiological Signal-Processing Framework for Network Physiology of Brain–Cardiorespiratory–Vascular Interactions: Application to N2 Sleep
content: Bridging the frequency gap between electroencephalogram (EEG) oscillatory activity and slower cardiorespiratory–vascular fluctuations is a fundamental signal-processing chal-lenge in Network Physiology. This study proposes a framework that represents EEG os-cillatory activity through slow fluctuations in band power, enabling integration with pe-ripheral physiological dynamics. Theta (θ, 4–8 Hz) and alpha (α, 8–13 Hz) band-power time series were extracted using Morlet wavelet transform (MWT) and integrated with R–R intervals (RRI), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and respiration in a five-variable multivari-ate autoregressive (MVAR) model. Frequency-dependent relative power contribution (RPC) quantified source-to-target predictive contributions and enabled visualization of directed network topologies in low-frequency (LF, 0.04–0.15 Hz) and high-frequency (HF, 0.15–0.50 Hz) bands. The framework was evaluated using simulated amplitude-modulated EEG signals and 16 six-minute segments of stage N2 non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep from six subjects. Simulations recovered the specified modulation frequencies, with repre-sentative correlations of 0.992 and 0.988 for θ and α power, respectively. In experimental recordings, 68.3% of θ- and 70.0% of α-band modulation power lay below 0.5 Hz. LF and HF topologies exhibited distinct contribution patterns. Notably, HF respiratory contribu-tions to SBP (28.1%) and RRI (16.4%) were prominent, consistent with established respira-tory–cardiovascular interactions during N2 sleep. EEG-derived variables also showed predictive contributions to peripheral physiological signals. These findings demonstrate a frequency-scale bridging approach for characterizing brain–cardiorespiratory–vascular network organization across different native oscillation frequencies.
